overview: Cedar Woods Properties is a Perth-headquartered national property developer, established in 1987 and ASX-listed since 1994, that develops residential land, townhouses, apartments and commercial properties across Western Australia, Victoria, Queensland and South Australia. The business operates a project-based development model spanning 36 active projects and a pipeline of over 9,600 undeveloped lots/units, generating revenue from land subdivision sales, built-form (townhouse/apartment) settlements, and a growing base of joint-venture and build-to-rent/commercial income. FY2026 (year ended 30 June 2026) delivered record NPAT of $65.6 million (up 36%) on revenue of $502.4 million (up 8%), with a record $830 million presales book underpinning FY2027 guidance of 15% NPAT growth.

business_model.summary: Cedar Woods buys and rezones/plans land, then earns development margin (~30% gross margin in FY2026) by subdividing and selling residential lots, and by constructing and settling townhouses, apartments and commercial/strata offices. Revenue is inherently lumpy and project/settlement-timing driven rather than recurring, though a large contracted presales book ($830m at 30 June 2026, ~65% expected to settle in FY27) provides multi-year earnings visibility. The company increasingly uses joint ventures (with government bodies, QIC and Tokyo Gas Real Estate Australia) to scale capital-efficiently and is expanding into build-to-rent and commercial/strata product to diversify beyond pure land subdivision. Growth capital is funded through operating cashflow, debt facilities and periodic equity issuance (shares on issue rose from 82.5m to 85.1m in FY2026, +3.1%) rather than buybacks.

revenue_streams.name: Residential land subdivision (WA, VIC, QLD, SA)
Joint venture / partnership projects (QIC, Tokyo Gas)

business_model.customer_type: B2C - owner-occupiers and investors purchasing residential lots, townhouses and apartments; some B2B for commercial/strata office and retail tenancies
business_model.geographic_mix: Western Australia (Perth) largest contributor, Victoria (Melbourne), Queensland (Brisbane/Gold Coast) and South Australia (Adelaide); 36 projects across the four states, no single state dominant enough to be sole driver

competitive_position.market_position: Mid-cap national developer, one of the more diversified players by state and product type but smaller in scale than majors like Stockland and Mirvac; particularly well-established and long-tenured in Western Australia

moat_factors.description: Pipeline of over 9,600 undeveloped lots/units across four states provides multi-year revenue visibility, though land itself is a commodity input available to any well-capitalised developer
Spread across WA, VIC, QLD and SA and across land/townhouse/apartment/commercial product cushions state-specific downturns, as demonstrated by WA/QLD strength offsetting VIC softness in FY2026

moat_factors.factor: Balance sheet discipline and track record
moat_factors.description: Conservative gearing (18.1% net debt/tangible assets, 8.1x interest cover, well within the 2x covenant) and a multi-decade record of consistent profitability support access to capital and JV partner trust through the cycle

moat_factors.factor: Institutional JV relationships (QIC, Tokyo Gas, government)
moat_factors.description: Repeat partnerships (three completed Tokyo Gas projects, a fourth approved; QIC at Robina) signal a reputational/execution advantage that allows capital-light access to larger sites
Established name since 1987 with rising customer NPS (+48, up 19 points in FY2026), but property development is largely a commodity business with limited switching costs or network effects

weaknesses: No structural moat typical of property development - land is fungible, buyers are price/location driven, and margins are set by the market cycle, not by CWP-specific advantages
Sub-scale relative to major diversified developers (Stockland, Mirvac), limiting bargaining power with contractors/suppliers
Reliant on third-party builders/contractors for construction delivery, exposing the company to contractor financial viability and capacity risk
Earnings are lumpy and settlement-timing dependent, complicating like-for-like comparisons and creating volatility in half-year results

growth_drivers: Record $830 million presales book at 30 June 2026, providing ~65% FY2027 settlement coverage and visibility into FY2028/FY2029

9,651-lot/unit development pipeline across WA, VIC, QLD and SA, including new acquisitions adding 1,184 lots/units in FY2026 (plus a further WA acquisition since year-end expanding Bushmead by 161 lots)
Accelerated/opportunistic land acquisition strategy exploiting the current cycle to secure future margin
Expansion of joint-venture/partnership model (QIC, Tokyo Gas Real Estate Australia) to scale capital-efficiently, including a fourth Tokyo Gas project (Subiaco) with planning approval received

Diversification into higher-density apartments, townhouses, build-to-rent-style community housing (e.g., Douglas Apartments, Noble Park - 97 apartments for community housing) and commercial/strata office product
Structural undersupply of Australian housing (National Housing Accord, Housing Australia Future Fund) providing medium-term demand support, particularly for affordable/mid-priced product
Anticipated RBA/Big-4-bank-forecast interest rate cuts in calendar 2027 expected to improve buyer borrowing capacity and reactivate demand

business.description: Earnings depend on residential sales volumes and prices across WA, VIC, QLD and SA metro markets; FY2026 saw a Q4 slowdown from rate rises, tax changes and consumer caution, with softer conditions expected to persist into FY2027

Civil contractors and builders face cost inflation, labour shortages and high work volumes under fixed-price contracts; contractor financial viability is an explicitly flagged elevated risk, particularly for apartment delivery

While diversified relative to single-state peers, CWP remains concentrated in WA/VIC/QLD/SA metro corridors and lacks NSW exposure; VIC underperformed in FY2026 on oversupply and weak consumer conditions
Growing reliance on QIC, Tokyo Gas and government JV partners introduces dependency on partner capital commitment, alignment and project-level decision sharing
Individual projects face rezoning, planning and environmental approval risk which can delay delivery and cash conversion

financial.risk: Rising net debt funding land acquisition
financial.description: Net bank debt rose 25.5% to $157.7m in FY2026 (gearing 18.1% of tangible assets, 29.0% debt/equity) to fund accelerated land purchases; still within the 20-75% target range and covenants (8.1x interest cover vs 2x covenant) but a trend to watch

financial.risk: Negative operating/free cash flow in expansion years
financial.description: FY2026 OCF was -$2.06m (operating cashflow before land acquisitions was +$97.0m) due to $99.1m of land investment; FCF has been negative in 7 of the last 12 annual periods, a structural feature of the development funding cycle rather than a profitability problem, but it constrains dividend/buyback flexibility in heavy-investment years

financial.risk: Interest rate exposure on unhedged debt
financial.description: Only 51% of drawn debt was hedged at 30 June 2026 (swaps/caps 3.3%-4.5%), leaving roughly half of borrowings exposed to further rate movements
No buyback program; shares on issue rose from 82.5m to 85.1m in FY2026 (+3.1%), diluting existing holders modestly to fund the acquisition pipeline

regulatory.risk: Federal tax policy changes affecting property investment
regulatory.description: Tax settings announced in the Federal budget contributed to buyer pausing in FY2026 Q4; property investment taxation remains a swing factor for investor demand
State and local planning regimes directly affect project timelines and feasibility across all four operating states
Bank capital and lending standards for home buyers directly affect the pool of qualified purchasers for CWP's products

macro.description: Successive interest rate rises through FY2026 weighed on buyer borrowing capacity and confidence; the FY2027 outlook depends on forecast (not certain) rate cuts materializing in calendar 2027

macro.risk: Consumer confidence and cost of living
macro.description: Geopolitical uncertainty (management specifically cited the Iran conflict) and cost-of-living pressures were cited as dampening buyer sentiment in FY2026 Q4
Elevated development costs and constrained construction sector capacity continue to compress project feasibility and delay delivery timeframes, particularly for apartments
Underlying demand is closely tied to population growth and immigration settings; a material slowdown would reduce structural housing demand

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australia's structural housing undersupply remains unresolved, with planning delays, infrastructure constraints, limited construction capacity and elevated development costs restricting new supply; this is expected to provide medium-term price/margin support, especially for affordable and mid-priced housing, even as near-term volumes soften
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - residential property development is one of the more cyclical sectors, sensitive to interest rates, credit availability, consumer confidence and government tax/housing policy; CWP's geographic and product diversification and large presales book smooth but do not eliminate this cyclicality
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - both directly (variable-rate debt funding costs, ~49% unhedged at FY2026 year end) and indirectly via buyer borrowing capacity and demand; management explicitly frames FY2027 guidance around anticipated RBA rate cuts

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year result released: record NPAT $65.6m (+36%), revenue $502.4m (+8%), gross margin 30% (up from 28%), EPS 77.9c (+33%), DPS 39.0c (+34%); shares jumped ~9.4% to $7.88 on the day
Management issued FY2027 guidance of 15% NPAT growth, backed by $830m in presales (~65% expected to settle in FY2027) and a 9,651 lot/unit pipeline across four states

Company flagged softer residential sales conditions expected through much of FY2027 due to Q4 FY2026 demand slowdown (interest rate rises, Federal budget tax changes, cost-of-living pressures, geopolitical uncertainty), while noting all Big-4 banks forecast rate cuts in calendar 2027
Board declared final fully franked dividend of 25.0 cents per share (total FY2026 dividends 39.0 cents, ~50% payout ratio); DRP/bonus share plan remains suspended
Contracted and settled a further WA land acquisition for $15.55 million, expanding the Bushmead estate by 161 residential lots
H1 FY2026 result: revenue $274.8m (+40% YoY), NPAT $39.6m (+164% YoY), reflecting settlement timing weighted to H1; corporate finance facility extension executed
Completed the third Tokyo Gas Real Estate Australia (TGREA) joint venture apartment project (SA) and received planning approval for a fourth TGREA project in Subiaco, WA

Commenced construction of Douglas Apartments, Noble Park (VIC) - 97 apartments for community housing plus retail - and Incontro apartments, Subiaco (WA); completed the Harrisdale Green JV with the WA State Government

New residential project launches included Somerley estate (VIC) and Sereno apartments (SA); land acquisitions added 1,184 lots/units to the pipeline, including expansions of the Flourish and Sage (QLD) projects

items.vs_prior: new guidance (FY2026 guidance was 30-35% NPAT growth, which FY2026 actual of 36.4% slightly exceeded)
items.notes: Underpinned by $830m presales book (~65% expected to settle in FY27) and a 9,651 lot/unit pipeline; management flagged softer residential sales conditions through much of FY2027 as a headwind risk to the outlook

items.target: Weighted to first half, similar to FY2026
items.notes: Reflects settlement timing across the presold project pipeline
FY2026 gross margin was 30%, up from 28% in FY2025, driven by improved sales prices, cost control and product mix

items.target: ~65% of $830m presales book to settle in FY2027, balance in FY2028/FY2029
items.notes: Several apartment projects contributing to FY2028/FY2029 earnings are under construction and well presold
FY2026 actual 29.0% net debt/equity, 18.1% net debt/total tangible assets less cash, comfortably within policy and covenants (8.1x interest cover vs 2x covenant)

guidance.management_commentary: Managing Director Nathan Blackburne said Cedar Woods enters FY2027 in a strong position with record presales, more than $120m of liquidity and a pipeline of over 9,600 lots/units across four states, but explicitly flagged expectations of softer residential sales conditions and ongoing construction sector challenges in parts of the country through much of FY2027. Chairman William Hames noted the operating environment is likely to remain variable near-term but characterized the balance sheet, diversified portfolio and experienced management team as a strong platform, while noting income tax changes announced in the Federal budget caused some purchasers to pause in the near term but are expected to support demand for new housing over the longer term.

bull_case: Record $830 million presales book provides unusually strong multi-year earnings visibility (65% locked in for FY2027 settlement) at a time many developers face demand uncertainty
Conservative balance sheet (18.1% gearing, 8.1x interest cover vs 2x covenant, $120m+ liquidity) gives capacity to keep acquiring land counter-cyclically while peers pull back
Structural Australian housing undersupply, National Housing Accord and government housing programs provide medium-term price/demand support, particularly for CWP's affordable/mid-priced niche

Diversification across four states and multiple product types (land, townhouses, apartments, commercial, JV/community housing) reduces single-market cyclicality, evidenced by WA/QLD strength offsetting VIC softness in FY2026

Expanding capital-efficient JV model with institutional partners (QIC, Tokyo Gas) plus potential RBA rate cuts in calendar 2027 could reaccelerate demand and support the 15% FY2027 NPAT growth target and beyond
bear_case: Property development has no durable moat - margins are ultimately set by the cycle, land is a commodity, and CWP is sub-scale versus majors like Stockland and Mirvac

Management itself flagged softening demand into FY2027 from elevated interest rates, cost-of-living pressure, geopolitical uncertainty and Federal tax changes, with FY2026 Q4 already showing a slowdown

Rising net debt (+25.5% YoY to $157.7m) and negative operating cash flow in 7 of the last 12 annual periods reflect a business that must continually reinvest to grow, limiting cash available for shareholder returns in expansion years

Construction sector capacity constraints, labour shortages and contractor financial-viability risk could delay apartment/townhouse deliveries and compress margins, especially given reliance on fixed-price building contracts
Growing dependence on JV partners (QIC, Tokyo Gas, government) for pipeline growth introduces execution and alignment risk that is harder for outside investors to monitor than wholly-owned projects
